text: You get a string of lowercase letters. Split it into as many parts as you can, so that each letter shows up in at most one part. Return the sizes of the parts, in order.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — the parts must be in order, and together they cover the whole string. So I'm really just picking where to cut. And if a letter is in one part, every copy of that letter must be in that same part. Is that right?
Yes. You only choose the cut points.

Okay. One thing I want to say early: a part must reach the last copy of every letter inside it. If a part has an a, it can't end before the last a. So the last position of each letter is the key fact here. Are there any constraints on the input size?
The length is between one and five hundred, and it's only lowercase English letters.

Got it. Only twenty-six letters, so there are at most twenty-six parts, and the sizes always add up to n. Let me check the first example. The long string gives nine, seven, eight. The first part, a-b-a-b-c-b-a-c-a, holds every a, b and c, and none of them show up later. Then the next two parts. Matches. The second example, e-c-c-b-b-b-b-d-e-c, gives ten: the last c is at the very end, so the first part has to run all the way. One part, size ten.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would try every set of cut points — two to the n minus one choices. Fine for ten letters, hopeless for five hundred. Rescanning each growing part is quadratic; it works, but we can do better. This problem reminds me of merging intervals. Each letter covers an interval, from its first copy to its last, and overlapping intervals must land in the same part. But a greedy scan with the last positions does the same job. I keep r, the furthest last position of any letter in this part — the earliest place it may end. When i reaches r, I cut. Cutting earlier splits a letter; cutting later only gives fewer parts. So cutting as soon as possible gives the most parts.
How sure are you that the greedy gives the most parts?

I checked it. I compared a brute force that tries every set of cut points against the greedy — every string over a, b, c up to length eleven, and every string over a, b, c, d up to length nine. Over six hundred thousand strings, zero mismatches, and the best split was always unique. So I'll go with the greedy.

Here's the plan, in three steps. First pass: record the last index of each letter in a twenty-six slot array. Second pass: walk left to right, pushing r out to the furthest last index in the current part. Third: when i equals r, record the size and start the next part right after r. One thing worth flagging — it must be max, not a plain overwrite. Take a-b-a. After the first a, r is two. The b's last index is one; overwrite, and r drops to one, cutting a-b off with an a still ahead. With max, r stays two and I get one part of size three. The end only grows. The trade-off: I could build and merge real intervals, but two passes with a small array is simpler and linear. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright. Two loops. The first just overwrites last for each letter, so the last write wins — the last index for free. The second pushes r out with max, and when i equals r it records r minus l plus one and moves l past r. One thing worth flagging — the order of those two lines matters: update r first, then check. I tested small changes against about one point four million short strings. Checking before updating breaks on a-a: one, one instead of two. Overwriting instead of max breaks on a-b-a. Setting l to r instead of r plus one breaks on a-b. Storing the first copy is wrong almost everywhere. Cosmetic variants, like greater-or-equal, are never wrong.

Let's dry-run example one: twenty-four letters, expected nine, seven, eight. Pass one puts the last a at eight, the last e at fifteen, the last j at twenty-three. The row that matters is i equals eight. Before it I only see b's and c's, whose last copies are at five and seven — inside eight, so r never moves. At eight I hit the last a, i equals r, and every letter so far is done. Cut, size nine. The other parts give seven and eight. Corner cases: a single letter gives one; five hundred of one letter gives five hundred; all twenty-six different gives twenty-six ones; e-c-c-b-b-b-b-d-e-c gives ten. Both examples pass, and fifty thousand random strings matched a quadratic reference.

Let me think about complexity here. There are two passes over the string, and each step is a lookup, a max and a compare. So time is linear. Space is constant extra: the last array is always twenty-six ints, and the answer has at most twenty-six parts. The worst case, like five hundred copies of one letter, is still just two passes. Oh, one more thing — the sizes always add up to n. The last cut always lands at the final index, because the last letter's last copy is the end of the string. So I never need a leftover part after the loop.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You reframed the problem early: a part must reach the last copy of every letter in it, so r is the earliest legal end, and cutting right there gives the most parts. You showed the two lines in the loop are not free to change — update with max first, then check — and a-b-a and a-a show what breaks. And you saw the space is constant, just twenty-six ints, with at most twenty-six parts. Good work.
